newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Europe power axis may turn on Swiss utility deals.
newsitem.headline: Europe power axis may turn on Swiss utility deals.

text.p: Two independent moves by Swiss utility concerns in the past three days have thrown open the door to new competition and alliances in Europe's power grid.

Union Bank of Switzerland said Sunday it will sell a total 40 percent stake in Swiss utility concern Motor-Columbus AG, with 20 percent going to Electricite de France International SA (EDF), and 20 percent to German utility (Rheinisch-Westfaelische Elektrizitaetswerk AG).
UBS said the move, if approved by authorities, will reduce its stake to 35.6 percent of the energy concern.
Motor-Columbus's main asset is ATEL (Aare-Tessin Electrizitaet), a major Swiss energy provider.
State-owned EDF said the stake in Motor-Columbus will cement not only a key source of power, but also a key partnership with RWE.
In an interview published Saturday by French newspaper Le Monde, EDF chairman Edmond Alphandery called the acquisition "part of a binding of ties among European electrical utilities."
He said Switzerland was pivotal for Europe, adding that ATEL controls nearly half of Swiss electricity exports.
EDF said that ATEL represented eight percent of Swiss sales, 13 percent of production, and 45 percent of sales abroad.

The news followed a separate announcement late Friday that another Swiss energy and industrial firm, Elektrowatt AG, plans to spin off its electricity activities, leaving it with a core of industrial businesses.
The electricity companies will be listed on the Swiss stock exchange as a new company, Watt AG, pending approval of shareholders at a general meeting set for February 19, 1997.

Further shifts in the balance of Europe's utilities powers are expected after the European Union agreed earlier this year to liberalisations which will gradually open up the European electricity market to more cross-border competition.
Analysts note that Switzerland's energy resources and geographic position present a mighty temptation to Europe's energy giants.
"Switzerland has a lot of hydropower, so their cost base has to be a lot lower," said one Swiss-based analyst, adding that the Swiss energy export sector also was highly profitable.
He compared the still-regionalised European utility sector to the telecommunications markets before deregulation, but said the energy sector's earnings potential might be more lucrative.

"It is probably a better market than telecommunications, because it has a better base of revenue, and a more stable base of revenue. The utility firms are highly capital-intensive. There is a lot of equity potential," he said.
After the Motor-Columbus sale, speculation could now revolve around the future ownership of both firms.
Traders on Swiss stock exchanges have long speculated that Motor-Columbus and Elektrowatt would merge.
The question may now be what the two utilities' respective major shareholders, two of Switzerland's largest banks, will do with their remaining stakes.
Swiss financial group CS Holding has a 44.9 percent stake in Elektrowatt.
CS has said earlier this year that it intends to sell its Elektrowatt stake, but has specified no timeframe. A CS spokesman had no comment on Elektrowatt's latest plans.
Separately, UBS said Sunday that "for the time being" it will retain the remaining 35.6 percent stake in Motor-Columbus.
According to Swiss media, for the moment at least a merger appears to be ruled out.
Oskar Ronner, president of Elektrowatt was quoted by the Swiss newspaper SonntagsZeitung on Sunday as saying: "We had already stated our interest in Motor-Columbus, now UBS has decided otherwise."
